/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.headline: Police and MI5 disrupt alleged plot against Manchester's Jewish community
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/charged-alleged-ter.bodyHtml:
A joint investigation by counter-terrorism police and MI5 has disrupted an alleged plot to attack Manchester’s Jewish community, leading to terrorism charges against two Iranian men.

Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner and the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism, said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”

Police say another man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with them as part of a plot to get a bomb to attack Jewish targets.

They were arrested two Sundays ago in broad daylight in a Manchester street during the Jewish holiday period.

Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police said the two men face charges that they gained materials and instructions to make a homemade bomb, identified possible targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack.

Police said: “It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot.”

Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.”

The development, terrorism charges and detail given so far by British authorities marks an extraordinary chapter in British and Iranian relations.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran had a link to a weekend scare at RAF Fairford when five men were arrested close to the military base, along with three vans, one of which contained petrol in a barrel. Those men have now been bailed, having been arrested in the early hours of Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing a terrorist act.

Evans added: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran.

“While this [Manchester] incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”

The alleged plot in Manchester, where the two arrests followed a joint counter-terrorism police and MI5 investigation, has significant potential ramifications on several fronts.

A government statement, minutes after the police announced the charges, revealed one of those accused over the Manchester plot had been granted asylum status in the UK and the other had an asylum application pending.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said that both of the accused had come to Britain via small boats, one in 2020 and another in 2023, when the Conservatives were in power.

Mahmood said Iran had shown hostile intent to the UK in a series of incidents.

“The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country,” she said. “While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.

“We will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security.

“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime. They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement.

“The prime minister has been clear there are strong indications of Iran’s involvement in the events near RAF Fairford. We are responding to these threats with new powers and record funding to disrupt hostile activity.

This week marked the anniversary of an attack on the Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester, where two worshippers died, as well as the attacker who said he supported Islamic State and was shot dead by police.

Jews in Britain have faced a dramatic increase in attacks since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, which has ties to Iran. It led to an internationally condemned military response by Israel in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people.

The Community Safety Trust, which offers security and advice to British Jews, said: “The charging of two men in connection with an alleged plot targeting the Manchester Jewish community will be deeply concerning to Jews across the UK.

“These charges come exactly a year after the appalling terrorist attack at Heaton Park synagogue, and are a reminder of the ongoing terrorist threats facing British Jews.

“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and report any suspicious activity to police and CST.”

In a statement, counter-terrorism police said the charges will allege the two men were “communicating with others using encrypted applications to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device”.

Furthermore, the charges allege they obtained a document called “Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb”, obtained video instructions on how to make an improvised explosive device (IED), and got the “liquids, components and equipment” to make an IED.

The charges also allege the men carried out internet research on targets, acquired “images, plans and maps of potential targets for attack” and carried out reconnaissance.

Iran has faced attack by the US, with Britain allowing the RAF Fairford base to be used, which it said is for defensive operations by its Washington ally. Tehran’s embassy in London this week denied any involvement in the events at RAF Fairford.

The men were arrested on 20 September in Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester’s city centre, just before 3pm, hours before Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Salehi and Ahmadyan are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October.

As part of the investigation officers raided and searched properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.

/education/2026/oct/02/school-inspection.headline: Lucy Powell acts to make Ofsted inspections fairer for disadvantaged schools
/education/2026/oct/02/school-inspection.bodyHtml:
School inspections in England are to be overhauled for the second time in a year, in response to a barrage of complaints that the new system was dangerously stressful and damaging teachers’ mental health.

Lucy Powell, the education secretary, will tell the schools regulator Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after becoming concerned that inspection changes overseen by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, were creating problems for headteachers.

Sources say Powell does not want to scrap the new system of ratings, which score schools from “exceptional” to needing “urgent improvement” in six key areas, but she does want inspectors to take greater account of the social and economic background of each school and its pupils.

Powell’s changes, which will be communicated to Ofsted in the coming weeks, will be the second set of major alterations to the school inspection regime in just over a year, after Labour’s election manifesto pledge to replace the previous inspection framework in the wake of the death of the headteacher Ruth Perry.

One source said: “She wants Ofsted to go back to the drawing board when it comes to measuring inclusion in particular. That’s where most of the problems seem to lie.”

Powell’s changes will mean a significant shift from those carried out by Phillipson, who is now equalities minister and party chair.

The two MPs fought an occasionally bitter contest to become Labour’s deputy leader last year, during which allies of each traded insults and accusations. Andy Burnham promoted Powell, a long-term ally, to Phillipson’s job as education secretary when he entered Downing Street earlier this year.

Powell told an event at last week’s Labour party conference: “I want to see a much stronger emphasis in the current inspection regime on context, much stronger than it is at the moment.

“I think this is one of those areas that it’s not straightforward to sort of move the oil tanker around massively quickly, but we absolutely do need to see reforms there.”

The inspectorate has commissioned its own independent evaluation of the new framework, with an interim report due out later this year; Ofsted declined to comment.

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said he was encouraged that ministers were listening to the criticism of inspections being raised by parents and experts as well as teachers.

Whiteman said: “We have serious concerns about fairness and comparability. Schools serve very different communities and face very different levels of challenge. Leaders working in areas of greater disadvantage, or with higher numbers of pupils with special educational needs (Send) and disabilities, must not be placed at a systemic disadvantage by an inspection framework that fails to properly reflect those contexts.

“Inspection should take account of the circumstances in which schools are operating, while recognising the tremendous work many are doing to support children facing the greatest barriers.

“There is a need for an inspection system that is rigorous and proportionate and which genuinely supports school improvement.”

The new “report card” system came into force last year, replacing Ofsted’s headline inspection grades of “outstanding” to “inadequate”, with a more detailed system intended to put less pressure on schools.

The new system was initially welcomed by teachers, though criticised by others who warned it would make it harder for parents to judge a school.

Since its implementation however, the regime has been met with a flurry of complaints from school leaders, who say it is harming their mental health and creating greater stress than the system it replaced.

Perry’s sister, Prof Julia Waters, said last month that she had been contacted by at least a dozen teachers left “feeling suicidal” by Ofsted inspections, and raised her concerns in a letter to the prime minister.

Amanda Hulme, the headteacher of Claypool primary school in Bolton, told the Guardian last month that her most recent Ofsted inspection was the most stressful experience of her career.

Unions have called for teachers to be given “urgent relief” from the new system, while some want Ofsted to stop grading their schools altogether.

A survey of school staff inspected under the new regime found that two-thirds said it was as bad or worse than the framework it had replaced. The survey of National Education Union members also found that three out of four said the inspections had negatively affected their mental health, with one primary school teacher describing it as “a circle of stress and fear”.

Powell is understood to be concerned that schools in more “challenging” contexts are doing worse under the new system.

A recent study by the former Ofsted inspector Steve Wren found schools with higher levels of children receiving free school meals (a key test of poverty) or Send support were receiving lower ratings than average.

Wren also found that ratings for secondary schools were closely correlated with how well pupils had performed before they joined the school, suggesting inspectors were not taking sufficient account of previous attainment levels.

Wren said in his analysis: “Do these grades represent the reality that secondary schools with lower prior attainment are doing a markedly worse job of educating their pupils, or is the framework biased against them, or are inspectors not skilled at spotting strengths in such contexts?”

/uk-news/2026/oct/02/ann-widdecombe-susp.headline: Detectives’ tireless work leads to new terror charge in Widdecombe case
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/ann-widdecombe-susp.bodyHtml:
A counter-terrorism investigation has led to a new charge against the man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe, with police saying he engaged in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism, including against Nigel Farage.

Counter-terrorism police said Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, relating to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year.

Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.

“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”

Police said Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.

She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.

“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”

A court previously heard that Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon.

Her gardener found her lying face down on her kitchen floor on the morning of 9 July, and emergency services declared her dead shortly afterwards.

Kerry is accused of her murder. At a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July, he spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address, and was not asked to indicate a plea.

Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.

“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.

“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”

Counter-terrorism police reopened a year-long investigation in August into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.

The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

After reopening the investigation, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.

/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.headline: Burnham to fund free national care service through pension reform
/politics/2026/oct/02/burnham-law-pensio.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham will fund a free national care service in England and a tax break for lower-income pensioners by changing the state pension triple lock during this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain in place until 2030, the government has said.

The prime minister used his conference speech to announce the change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth.

In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to prevent much larger pension increases in years when wages spike.

In his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee.

Guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, giving MPs a vote on the changes.

It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether to retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power.

The guidance also shows that the government expects the change to save £15bn a year in state pension spending by the end of the 2030s, rising to £50bn a year by 2050.

However, the Resolution Foundation said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model.

Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s.

“Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings.

“If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.”

Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly.

Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care changes would be “electoral suicide”.

However, YouGov has published polling suggesting voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.

In his speech, Burnham confirmed he would end the pension triple lock and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.

He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation.

Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.

/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.headline: Quick-thinking passengers and off-duty pilots save flydubai flight
/world/2026/oct/02/aviation-security-fly.bodyHtml:
At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.

Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.

Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.

Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”

Much about what happened on flight FZ 1073 is still unclear, but details of what happened next — how the flight was saved — are well documented by witness testimony and videos.

A small group of passengers rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot, one of them a plumber who copied a manoeuvre he had seen on television documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive. The plane had gone into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, and most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children.

Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.

In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.

Even as his strength ebbed, the pilot managed to unlock the cockpit security door, having already sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack.

“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”

For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.

The co-pilot was barred from flying in Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, the Associated Press quoted a source as saying on Saturday, and was subsequently hired by flydubai.

In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.

“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.

Experts said there have been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.

In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.

Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.

“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”

There has, though, been limited evidence so far that violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the war in Gaza, even as security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the conflict, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago.

Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.

“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”

Machchhar’s desperate efforts allowed access to the flight deck, enabling passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and off-duty pilots to bring the plane in to land; if those efforts had failed, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died. The episode has still raised many questions for aviation security, including the long-controversial decision, taken after 9/11, to let pilots lock cockpit doors from the inside.

There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.

Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”

Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.

“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.

The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.

Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.

Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

/uk-news/2026/oct/02/palestine-action-ac.headline: Palestine Action activists stand trial over alleged raid on arms factory
/uk-news/2026/oct/02/palestine-action-ac.bodyHtml:
Five Palestine Action activists are standing trial accused of brandishing whips, hammers and kebab skewers to intimidate security guards and keep them at bay during a break-in at an Israel-linked arms factory, a court has heard.

Prosecutors allege the five defendants were part of a “black team”, wearing black jumpsuits, whose role was to overwhelm security guards so that a “red team”, wearing red jumpsuits, could break into the Elbit systems factory in Filton, near Bristol, and smash up equipment including drones.

Qesser Zuhrah, 21, Zahra Farooque, 26, Kamran Ahmed, 29, Heba Muraisi, 31, and Liam Mullany, 34, deny criminal damage and violent disorder over the raid during the early hours of 6 August 2024, and their trial opened at Woolwich crown court on Friday.

The prosecutor Deanna Heer KC told the jury that an alleged plan of the raid, discovered by police, said: “Shut Elbit Down. This is our primary objective as Palestine Action. We can do that by sticking together and ensuring its destruction with our brains and muscle.”

Jurors heard that the security guard, Nigel Shaw, struck a member of the black team across the back of his legs with an umbrella before suffering a 4cm laceration to his head after being attacked.

Heer said: “The role of the black team was to overwhelm the security guards so that the red team could break into the factory. They did so by threatening, intimidating and, if necessary, assaulting the guards, by throwing fireworks at them and brandishing weapons, such as whips and hammers and large kebab skewers.

“When one of the black team was detained by a security guard, other members of the group attacked him, hitting him until he released their colleague, leaving the security guard with a laceration to his head.”

She told the court the break-in was carefully planned and a prison van, driven by a member of the red team, crashed through the first perimeter fence surrounding Elbit’s factory at about 3.30am.

The black team followed on foot shouting slogans including “Free Palestine” as the van was driven through a second perimeter fence at the site of the firm, whose parent company is based in Israel.

Heer said: “The footage shows that the black team used or threatened violence against the security guards that night. It is clear, the prosecution submit, that Nigel Shaw was physically attacked and [was] caused injury but violence was also used or threatened by the black team before then when they threw fireworks or smoke grenades or cracked whips and brandished skewers in order to intimidate the security guards and keep them away.”

She said the idea was for the red team to destroy “as much property as possible” before the police arrived and they used fire extinguishers filled with red paint to spray the walls and floor, crowbars and sledgehammers to smash apart computer equipment and drones and also damaged a disabled toilet.

The court was told that the plan for the break-in described the black team, who had their faces covered, as “coverts” because the intention was “to get away without being caught”, unlike the red team who were labelled “overts”.

The trial continues.

/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.headline: Thousands march for democracy in Rio as Lula seeks fourth term
/world/2026/oct/02/brazil-lula-stop-fasc.bodyHtml:
The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a huge pro-democracy rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election, telling supporters he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power.

Speaking on the eve of the rally, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could stop the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.

“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lula told a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”

Hours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.

“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.

Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”

From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.

“No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.

The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places reflected how this year’s election has stirred renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.

Jair Bolsonaro, the ex-president and father of Lula’s rival, is already serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election; election-eve polls suggest Lula now holds only a slender lead over his son, Flávio.

Many Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.

“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.

Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”

Valmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”

Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable.”

“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”

During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.

Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.

“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.

Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”

At Friday’s rally, Lula said he could pull off a shock first-round win by securing more than 50 per cent of the vote, even though polls suggest the contest is more likely to go to a second-round runoff on 25 October, with Lula on about 45 per cent against Bolsonaro’s 40 per cent, according to the Datafolha pollster.

In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.

/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.headline: French students make the case for better schools in nationwide protests
/world/2026/oct/02/student-protests-shut.bodyHtml:
Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of a barricade of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, standing alongside dozens of fellow pupils instead of attending her usual Spanish class.

Now on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of other pupils, ensuring all lessons were cancelled, the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published, said: “We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement. We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”

“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia set out the grievances driving teenagers across France to speak up: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June.

Several teachers stood by the barricades in support of the pupils. “The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation, adding that she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week.

Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected, and the French government is now facing its biggest crisis in months after being taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested, with the movement set to continue into next week.

Many of the protesting students have spoken out about the state’s disengagement from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.

The government acknowledged that the grievances were legitimate, while condemning what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.

An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw, after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher; the family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”. Several other students have also been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals.

“We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published, as riot police stood guard on Friday outside Lycée Voltaire amid a quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade, and wanted to study catering next year.

“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”

On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.”

Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”

Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.

Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special €1 meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”

He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”

/world/2026/oct/03/bangkok-thailand-floo.headline: Bangkok residents band together as authorities drain floodwaters
/world/2026/oct/03/bangkok-thailand-floo.bodyHtml:
Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.

Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters set up across the city, authorities said, as the government reported that about 40 people had died in flood-related incidents. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution.

Every city has a breaking point, though, and this year rain fell so fast and hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital were transformed, not into rivers, but into stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.

Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground-floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, ‘like all day, all night’.

‘The water just kept rising,’ said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high.

Authorities had managed to drain away the worst of the flooding by Thursday at the 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok, where Suleemas lives and which has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared across Thailand of the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface.

Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. ‘People are so happy to see the sunshine,’ she said. ‘Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.’

Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope.

The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man was arrested for riding a jetski along a main road.

‘It’s a lesson,’ said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. ‘The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the “end of the world” is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.’

Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage to pile up and forcing flight cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home.

Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, said a war room had been set up to monitor the situation, while telling reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from the north. Thailand’s weather agency has forecast more heavy rain for next week.

It is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force.

‘In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,’ said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who has studied heavy rain in the region. ‘In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.’

It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed.

The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strong El Niño, a cyclical weather pattern that brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall.

Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authored a study on Bangkok’s flood resilience, said the city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but that localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress. He said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days.

‘The government did not communicate the seriousness,’ said Laeni. ‘Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.’

Neighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country.

Rescuers were pulling bodies from a landslide that devastated the village of Ka Det Nge Htein in Myanmar’s south at the weekend. That disaster had already claimed nine lives, and eight more people are missing under the mud in another village, local officials said.

Civil war across the country, and a junta that restricts the media, have made it hard to get information, and hampered aid organisations.

Back in Bangkok, pumping stations have been operating at full capacity, though it could be days before the waters fully drain.

At her apartment complex, Suleemas said she would stay where she was with her neighbours.

‘It’s hard, yes, very hard,’ she said. ‘But together we are fighting and biting through it. When we get together to help one another like this, our spirit can keep us on our feet; we can get through it all together.’

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report
